newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Witness says S.Africa's Zulu chief used hit-squads.
newsitem.headline: Witness says S.Africa's Zulu chief used hit-squads.

text.p: A witness to South Africa's truth probe said on Wednesday top secret military documents showed Zulu leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi used state- trained hit-squads to turn a political conflict in his favour.

A special truth hearing into covert apartheid-era military training of 200 Inkatha Freedom Party men loyal to Buthelezi was presented with extracts from the military documents detailing the relationship between Buthelezi and the military.

The extracts were contained in a submission by Howard Varney, the former civilian head of a unit probing hit-squads in KwaZulu-Natal where the trainees were deployed in 1986 to fight supporters of the African National Congress (ANC).

"According to military documents drawn up in February 1988, Buthelezi reportedly called for more Inkatha members to be trained in order to swing the conflict in the townships in his favour," Varney told the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
"The government viewed Inkatha as a bulwark against internal revolution and took steps to build up Inkatha as an anti-revolutionary force," he added.
The state was fighting against the then-banned ANC and its internal ally, the United Democratic Front (UDF), which were trying to overthrow apartheid.

Buthelezi -- who has declined to testify before the truth commission -- said through his lawyer earlier in the day that he had no knowledge of any hit-squad killings in his province and was "astounded" by the allegations.
"Many high-profile people in this country are being implicated in these hearings. Once these cases are stated they cause irreparable damage," lawyer Patrick Falconer added.

The powerful State Security Council (SSC), which comprised senior government ministers and security force officers and deliberated on matters of state, had noted the rising tension between Inkatha and UDF.

"During 1985 the expressed mutual hostility and mistrust between Inkatha and the UDF became a visible reality when Inkatha realised that the UDF represented a threat to its power monopoly in KwaZulu and decided...that (KwaZulu-Natal) be turned into a so-called 'no-go area' for the UDF, regardless of the consequences," a SSC document said.
Three hit-squad members have told the truth commission they were trained specifically to kill their political opponents and protect their leaders from attacks by the ANC and UDF.

"While the political leaders of the South African government and Inkatha may not have been aware of the individual actions carried out, they are accountable for the murders and atrocities that flowed from the project," Varney said in his testimony.
Some 15,000 people have been killed in over a decade of fighting in KwaZulu-Natal between Inkatha and the ANC.
The truth commission was set up by President Nelson Mandela to probe apartheid-era crimes committed by both sides and foster reconciliation through confession and apology.
